lesson.title: From Schematic to Bench: Why Engineers Prototype
lesson.summary: Prototyping is the practice of building a real, temporary physical version of a circuit before committing to a permanent one, because a schematic drawing cannot reveal every way real components and real construction will behave.
lesson.body:
A schematic, built out of the standard circuit schematic symbols you already know, is a plan. It tells you exactly how the resistors, capacitors, inductors, and other components are supposed to connect, and if you trust the ideal models of those components, you can predict on paper exactly how the circuit will behave. Prototyping is the step of actually building that plan out of real physical parts on a bench, before you commit to a permanent version, in order to check whether the real circuit agrees with the paper prediction.

The reason this step is necessary, rather than skippable, is that real components are not perfectly ideal, and a schematic diagram cannot show you the ways they fall short. A real resistor has a tolerance, meaning its actual value might sit a few percent away from the number printed on it, and it has a maximum power rating that a schematic symbol never displays. A real capacitor has some small internal resistance in series with its ideal capacitance, called equivalent series resistance, which a purely theoretical capacitor symbol does not capture, along with leakage and a voltage rating it cannot safely exceed. A real inductor has resistance in its winding wire, which causes it to behave partly like a resistor as well as an inductor, and its core can saturate and stop behaving as expected if driven with too much current. None of these non ideal behaviors show up in the clean symbols on a schematic, and they can be the exact reason a circuit that looks perfect on paper does not work quite right on the bench.

Prototyping is also simply the fastest way to catch ordinary mistakes: a wire connected to the wrong node, a resistor value that was miscalculated, a stage of the circuit that oscillates or behaves unexpectedly once real, imperfect parts are involved. Finding these problems on a temporary, easily modified prototype is vastly cheaper and faster than discovering them after a circuit has been permanently assembled.

There are two common ways to build a physical prototype, and each has its own chapter following this one. A breadboard lets you insert component leads into a reusable grid of spring clips with no soldering at all, making it fast to build and just as fast to change, ideal for the earliest, most exploratory stage of testing an idea. Soldering onto a board makes the connections permanent, appropriate once a design built and tested on a breadboard has proven itself and is ready for a more durable, reliable build. Both are prototyping in the sense described here: a real, physical stand in for the schematic, built specifically so you can test before you commit.
